newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Negotiators say world telecoms deal on track.
newsitem.headline: Negotiators say world telecoms deal on track.

text.p: A global pact to liberalise the $600 billion telecoms trade is on track ahead of Saturday's deadline, boosted by new offers from Canada and the European Union to open up markets further, negotiators said on Wednesday.

The EU tabled a final and more liberal proposal and Canada offered to ease controls on its domestic satellite market, while more countries were expected to revise offers listing how far they are ready to open domestic markets to outside competition.
"We can relatively confidently say that we look forward to a successful conclusion to the talks by the end of this week," the European Union chief negotiator Karl Falkenberg told reporters.
"I don't expect any difficulties as long as everything that is on the table today is on the table on Saturday. Hopefully we can all go home and even do some skiing on Saturday."
Major trading partners were still looking for last-minute improvements in proposals from nations including Canada, Mexico and Korea but main problems appeared to have been solved.
Falkenberg said the focus had now switched to countries outside the world's four main trading partners -- the United States, the EU, Canada and Japan -- or the so-called "Quad".
The United States and the European Union each represent roughly a third of the global revenue on telecoms markets, followed by Japan with a 15 percent share.
"As of today, we have well over 90 percent of the world revenue in telecoms covered by offers of different participants," Falkenberg said.
"We certainly think this is an achievement that would make it impossible for members not to conclude the talks."

Some 59 governments representing more than 90 per cent of the global market have submitted offers to open their domestic telecom markets to foreign operators. Sri Lanka and Tanzania were expected to present offers by the end of the week.
A global pact will dramatically cut consumers' telecoms bills, secure a fair playing field and pave the way for mergers in a more competitive industry, Falkenberg said.
One sticking point for Washington was the level of opening to foreign ownership of telecoms companies offered by Canada, which allows a maximum 47.8 percent foreign equity holding.

Senior Canadian trade officials ruled out any change in their stance on Wednesday but instead offered to relax a law requiring the use of Canadian satellites only for domestic satellite communications and bring foreign operators on board.
They too expressed optimism that a deal would be clinched.

"The European Union believes there's a deal to be had here, Japan believes there's a deal to be had here and Canada and most other countries believe there's a deal," said a senior Canadian trade official.

U.S. negotiators are now conducting an assessment of whether they have the "critical mass" of quality offers Washington says it needs to guarantee unfettered foreign access to is own telecoms market, the world's biggest.

The U.S. assessment is vital as the United States is the world's biggest telecoms market and last April derailed a previous talks on a deal, when it walked away arguing that there was not a "critical mass" of good offers on the table.
There was no word from the U.S. delegation on Wednesday, but Falkenberg said he thought Washington would not give thumbs-down to a final pact because of discontent with Canada's offer.

"I think the United States is coming round to a more rational approach. "Canada is opening access to its markets in a different number of ways. I have the impression we are not going to see this issue become a deal-breaker," he said.
"I think the Americans are in a very different mood today than they were in April 1996. I think they have realised the important clarifications and improvements we have achieved."
